cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf types, with small-leaf plants at Yibang
processing: Sun-dried maocha, pressed or sold loose; the same region also supplies leaf for ripe tea, which is a separate category.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking; the climate has a dry season from November to April and a wet one from May to October, so the rainy summer leaf is the least valued.
appearance_dry: Large, dark olive leaf with silvery buds in good grades, though this varies by mountain.
appearance_liquor: Clear gold when young, moving to amber with age.
appearance_wet: Thick, supple large leaves in most lots.
taste_profile: No single flavour: Yiwu is soft and sweet with floral-fruity notes and little bitterness, while Bulang's Laobanzhang is known as the region's most famous and much stronger tea.

brewing.notes: Adjust to the mountain: a Yiwu takes longer steeps happily, while a Bulang tea needs them shorter.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year and, increasingly, by mountain or village. A cake labelled only Xishuangbanna or Banna is usually a blend or modest regional leaf, and it is priced accordingly. Young cakes are drunk within a few years or stored for ageing; serious old sheng from here is sold with its year stated.
description:
Xishuangbanna is the southernmost part of Yunnan, on the borders of Laos and Myanmar, and the historic centre of pu-erh. As a tea name it means a whole region rather than one style, covering the Six Ancient Tea Mountains and famous villages such as Laobanzhang.

The climate is warm and wet with a dry winter and a monsoon summer. Sheng from here follows the usual path of sun-dried maocha and pressing, and the leaf is mostly large-leaf material, which gives it the weight pu-erh is known for.

The range is wide. Yiwu teas are soft and sweet, Mahei is held up as the clearest example of that style, and Bulang teas lean strong and bitter with a long return. Brew with the mountain in mind instead of using one routine for the whole region.

A regional label tells you only the broad origin. For anything more specific, look for a stated mountain or village, a harvest year, and a clear statement of tree age.
history:
The Six Ancient Tea Mountains, Yiwu, Youle, Gedeng, Yibang, Manzhuan and Mangzhi, made this area the core of the Qing-era pu-erh trade, with Yiwu acting as a main collecting point for leaf bound for Pu'er prefecture. In 1729 the Qing court split the lands east of the Lancang River off into the new Pu'er prefecture.

The modern autonomous prefecture dates from the 1950s. Interest in single-mountain tea grew much later, shifting attention from regional blends to individual villages.
